days.title: CloudWatch Metrics and Alarms Fundamentals

concepts.heading: Metric namespaces and dimensions
concepts.body: CloudWatch metrics are organized into namespaces (such as AWS/EC2 or a custom application namespace) and further split by dimensions, which are key-value pairs like InstanceId or Environment that let you filter and aggregate the same metric name in different ways. AWS services publish default metrics automatically at a fixed resolution (usually every 1 or 5 minutes), while applications can publish custom metrics with the PutMetricData API at standard or high resolution (down to 1 second). On the exam, remember that CPUUtilization for EC2 is a default metric, but anything like memory usage or a business KPI requires a custom metric published by an agent or your own code.

concepts.heading: Alarm states and evaluation periods
concepts.body: A CloudWatch alarm watches a single metric (or a math expression) against a threshold over a configurable number of evaluation periods, and transitions between three states: OK, ALARM, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA when not enough data points exist yet. You tune sensitivity with the evaluation period length, the number of periods that must breach the threshold, and datapoints-to-alarm settings, trading off fast detection against false positives from short spikes. Alarms can trigger actions directly, including publishing to an SNS topic, invoking an Auto Scaling policy, or executing an EC2 action such as stop, terminate, reboot, or recover.

concepts.heading: EC2 automatic recovery via alarms
concepts.body: When an EC2 instance fails its underlying hardware-level status check (not the software-level instance status check), a CloudWatch alarm configured with the recover action can automatically migrate the instance to new hardware while preserving its instance ID, private IP, and EBS volumes. This is a key operational pattern for stateful workloads that cannot simply be replaced by Auto Scaling, since recovery keeps the same instance rather than launching a new one. It only works for instance types and configurations that support recovery, so scenario questions about single, non-Auto-Scaled instances that must self-heal usually point here.

concepts.heading: Composite alarms for noise reduction
concepts.body: A composite alarm combines the states of multiple underlying alarms using AND/OR/NOT logic, so it only enters ALARM when a more specific combination of conditions is true, such as high CPU AND high request latency at the same time. This is the standard answer whenever a scenario describes too many individual alarm notifications or wants to suppress alerts unless several signals agree, reducing alert fatigue for on-call engineers. Composite alarms do not replace the underlying alarms; they sit on top of them and are evaluated based on the states those alarms already report.

concepts.heading: CloudWatch dashboards for shared visibility
concepts.body: Dashboards let you pin multiple metric graphs, alarms, and even logs widgets onto a single customizable view that can be shared across a team or displayed on a NOC screen, giving everyone the same real-time picture of operational health. Dashboards can span multiple regions and accounts (with cross-account observability configured), which matters for organizations running workloads across several AWS accounts. They are purely visualization; they do not themselves generate alerts, so a dashboard is never the right answer when the question asks for automatic notification or remediation.

examPoints: A question describing an instance that must self-heal after a hardware failure, keeping the same instance ID, is pointing to a CloudWatch alarm with the EC2 recover action, not Auto Scaling replacement.
A scenario about reducing noisy alerts by requiring multiple conditions to be true at once is describing a composite alarm, not a single alarm with a stricter threshold.

quiz.q: An EC2 instance running a legacy application must automatically recover on the same instance ID if the underlying hardware fails, without being replaced by a new instance. What should the operations engineer configure?
choices: An Auto Scaling group with a minimum capacity of 1
A CloudWatch alarm on the instance status check with the Recover action
An Elastic Load Balancer health check
quiz.explain: The CloudWatch alarm Recover action migrates the instance to new hardware while preserving its instance ID and attached volumes; Auto Scaling would launch a brand-new instance instead, which does not meet the 'same instance' requirement.

quiz.q: An operations team wants a single notification only when both CPU utilization and request latency are simultaneously elevated, ignoring brief spikes in either metric alone. Which CloudWatch feature should they use?
choices: A single alarm with a very high threshold
A composite alarm combining the two underlying alarms with AND logic
A CloudWatch dashboard with both metrics displayed
Increasing the evaluation period on one alarm
quiz.explain: A composite alarm evaluates the states of multiple alarms with logical operators, firing only when the combined condition is met; a single alarm cannot evaluate two independent metrics with AND logic.

days.recap: CloudWatch metrics come from default AWS publishing or custom PutMetricData calls; alarms transition states on threshold breaches and can trigger SNS, Auto Scaling, or EC2 recovery actions; composite alarms cut noise by combining conditions.

days.title: Centralized Logging and Event-Driven Automation

concepts.heading: CloudWatch Logs subscription filters
concepts.body: A subscription filter watches a log group in real time and forwards any log event matching a defined pattern (such as the literal string ERROR or a JSON-based filter pattern) to a destination like a Lambda function, Kinesis Data Stream, or Amazon Data Firehose (formerly Kinesis Data Firehose). This turns log analysis from a manual, after-the-fact activity into an event-driven pipeline, so an application error can trigger an automated notification or remediation action within seconds of being written. A common exam trap is choosing CloudTrail here instead of CloudWatch Logs — CloudTrail records API calls, while subscription filters operate on arbitrary application or system log content.

concepts.heading: CloudWatch Logs Insights for ad hoc analysis
concepts.body: Logs Insights provides a purpose-built query language for interactively searching and aggregating data across one or more CloudWatch Logs log groups, letting you compute things like the count of errors per five-minute bucket or the slowest requests in a time range without exporting data anywhere else. Because queries run directly against ingested logs, there is no separate ETL step, making it well suited for quickly diagnosing an incident while it is still happening. It is read-only analysis, though — it does not trigger anything by itself, so any requirement for automatic action still needs an alarm or EventBridge rule layered on top.

concepts.heading: EventBridge rules for automated remediation
concepts.body: EventBridge rules match on the structure of events from AWS services (EC2 state changes, GuardDuty findings, Config compliance changes) or custom applications, and route matching events to targets such as Lambda functions, SSM Automation documents, or SNS topics. This is the backbone of auto-remediation pipelines: for example, a GuardDuty finding indicating a compromised instance can trigger an EventBridge rule that immediately invokes an SSM Automation runbook to isolate the instance by changing its security group, with no human in the loop. Distinguish this from CloudWatch alarms, which react to metric thresholds, whereas EventBridge reacts to discrete state-change events.

concepts.heading: EventBridge Scheduler for recurring operations
concepts.body: EventBridge Scheduler lets you invoke a target on a one-time or recurring basis using cron or rate expressions, replacing ad hoc cron jobs on individual servers with a fully managed, serverless scheduling service. It supports millions of independently configured schedules and features like flexible time windows and automatic retries, which makes it a better fit than a single EventBridge rule (formerly CloudWatch Events) when you need many distinct per-tenant or per-resource schedules. Typical operational use cases include nightly batch jobs, periodic health checks, and scheduled scaling actions outside of Auto Scaling's own scheduled actions.

concepts.heading: Choosing the right trigger mechanism
concepts.body: When a scenario asks how to react to something, the mechanism depends on the signal type: a numeric metric crossing a threshold calls for a CloudWatch alarm, a specific log line appearing calls for a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter, and a discrete AWS service event (a finding, a state change, an API call pattern) calls for an EventBridge rule. Many real architectures chain these together, for instance an alarm publishing to SNS which is itself an EventBridge-compatible target, or a subscription filter feeding Lambda which then emits a custom EventBridge event for further routing. Recognizing which trigger category a question describes is often the fastest way to eliminate wrong answers.

examPoints: When a scenario says a specific error string appearing in application logs should trigger an immediate Lambda invocation, the answer is a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter, not CloudWatch alarms or CloudTrail.
When a scenario describes a GuardDuty finding automatically triggering an isolation workflow with no human intervention, the answer is an EventBridge rule targeting Lambda or SSM Automation.

quiz.q: An application writes 'ERROR' to its CloudWatch log group whenever a critical failure occurs, and the operations team wants an SNS notification sent within seconds of that happening. What should they configure?
choices: A CloudWatch alarm on a custom metric filter with a long evaluation period
A CloudWatch Logs subscription filter forwarding matching events to a Lambda function that publishes to SNS
A CloudTrail trail with a lifecycle policy
A Config rule for log group compliance
quiz.explain: A subscription filter delivers matching log events in near real time to a target such as Lambda, which can then publish to SNS immediately; a metric filter with an alarm typically has a coarser evaluation period, making it slower for single-event detection.

quiz.q: GuardDuty detects a compromised EC2 instance and the security team wants the instance automatically isolated by an SSM Automation runbook without any manual approval step. Which service should route the finding to the runbook?
quiz.explain: EventBridge rules can match on GuardDuty finding events and invoke SSM Automation as a target, forming an automated remediation pipeline; Config tracks resource configuration compliance, not security findings.

days.recap: Subscription filters push matching log lines to Lambda/Kinesis in real time; Logs Insights is for interactive log queries; EventBridge rules react to discrete AWS events for automated remediation; Scheduler replaces cron for recurring managed jobs.

days.title: Auditing and Configuration Compliance with CloudTrail and Config

concepts.heading: CloudTrail as the account activity record
concepts.body: CloudTrail records nearly every API call made in an AWS account, capturing the identity of the caller, the source IP, the timestamp, the request parameters, and the response, which makes it the primary tool for answering 'who did what and when.' Management events (control-plane operations like creating a security group) are logged by default and retained for 90 days at no charge in Event history, but a trail delivering events to an S3 bucket is needed for longer retention, cross-region aggregation, or forwarding to CloudWatch Logs for alerting. Data events (like individual S3 object-level API calls or Lambda invocations) are higher volume and must be explicitly enabled because they incur additional cost.

concepts.heading: Large-scale SQL analysis of CloudTrail events
concepts.body: CloudTrail Lake, a managed event data store for running SQL directly against CloudTrail events, has been closed to new customers since 2026-05-31, and AWS now recommends Amazon CloudWatch for capturing, storing, and analyzing CloudTrail logs. In practice, send a trail to CloudWatch Logs and query it with CloudWatch Logs Insights (which supports SQL as well as its own query language), or query the trail's S3 archive with Amazon Athena for long-term history. This is the right answer when a scenario specifically calls for SQL-based querying of audit history over long retention periods with minimal operational overhead. Either way, the trail itself remains the foundation for near-real-time alerting and durable retention.

concepts.heading: AWS Config for continuous configuration tracking
concepts.body: AWS Config records the configuration state of supported resources over time and maintains a configuration history, so you can see exactly how a resource's settings looked at any past point, not just whether an API call happened. Config Rules (AWS-managed or custom, written in Lambda or Guard) continuously evaluate resources against desired conditions, such as requiring that every S3 bucket block public access, and mark resources as COMPLIANT or NON_COMPLIANT. This is fundamentally different from CloudTrail: Config answers 'what does this resource look like and has it always met policy,' while CloudTrail answers 'who changed it.'

concepts.heading: Automated remediation with Config
concepts.body: Config Rules can be attached to a remediation action, typically an SSM Automation document, so that a non-compliant resource is automatically corrected — for example, automatically re-enabling S3 Block Public Access when a rule detects it was disabled. Remediation can be configured to require manual approval or to run fully automatically, and you can limit retry attempts to avoid remediation loops on a resource that keeps drifting. This pairs Config's detective capability with SSM's corrective capability, forming a closed-loop compliance system that needs no daily manual review.

concepts.heading: Using CloudTrail and Config together for full audit coverage
concepts.body: Because CloudTrail shows the API call that caused a change and Config shows the resulting configuration state before and after, combining them lets you fully reconstruct an incident: Config flags that a security group became non-compliant, and CloudTrail's event history around that timestamp reveals which IAM principal made the API call. Exam scenarios that ask for both 'what changed' and 'who changed it' are testing whether you know you need both services rather than either one alone. Aggregating both into a multi-account, multi-region setup (via CloudTrail organization trails and Config aggregators) is standard practice for centralized governance.

examPoints: A scenario asking who modified a specific security group rule and when is asking for CloudTrail, since it records the identity and timestamp of API calls.
A scenario asking whether resources continuously satisfy a policy such as 'no public S3 buckets,' with alerts on drift, is asking for AWS Config Rules, not CloudTrail.

quiz.q: A security team needs to determine which IAM user modified a security group's inbound rules at 2:15 PM yesterday. Which service provides this information?
quiz.explain: CloudTrail logs the calling identity, source IP, and timestamp for the API call that modified the security group; Config would show the resulting configuration change but not necessarily identify the caller as directly as CloudTrail does.

quiz.q: An organization wants every S3 bucket to be continuously checked for public access settings, with automatic notification whenever a bucket becomes non-compliant. What should they configure?
choices: A CloudTrail trail with a subscription filter
AWS Config with a managed rule and an SNS notification on compliance change
A CloudWatch alarm on S3 request metrics
quiz.explain: Config Rules continuously evaluate resource configuration against policy and can notify on compliance state changes; CloudTrail only logs discrete API calls rather than continuously evaluating current state.

days.recap: CloudTrail answers who called which API and when; Config tracks configuration history and evaluates continuous compliance via Config Rules; Config Rules plus SSM Automation remediation closes the loop automatically.

days.title: Remote Operations at Scale with Systems Manager

concepts.heading: Run Command for fleet-wide execution
concepts.body: Systems Manager Run Command executes predefined or custom commands and scripts across many EC2 instances or on-premises servers simultaneously, entirely over the SSM Agent channel, without needing SSH keys, bastion hosts, or open inbound ports. Command output, execution status per instance, and rate controls (how many instances run concurrently, and error thresholds that halt the rollout) are all managed centrally, which makes it the standard way to apply a one-off operational change like restarting a service or collecting a diagnostic file across hundreds of hosts at once. It is a good fit for simple, single-step actions; multi-step orchestrated workflows are better served by Automation.

concepts.heading: Systems Manager Automation for multi-step runbooks
concepts.body: Automation runs SSM documents (runbooks) written as ordered steps that can branch, wait, and call across services, enabling workflows such as create an AMI, launch a replacement instance from it, verify health, then terminate the old instance, all without a human clicking through each stage. AWS provides many prebuilt automation documents (like AWS-RestartEC2Instance or documents for patching workflows) and you can author custom ones in YAML or JSON, version them, and invoke them from EventBridge rules for full auto-remediation pipelines. The distinguishing exam signal is a multi-step, ordered operational procedure — that phrasing almost always means Automation rather than plain Run Command.

concepts.heading: Session Manager for secure interactive access
concepts.body: Session Manager provides a browser- or CLI-based interactive shell to a managed instance using IAM permissions alone, requiring no SSH key pairs, no bastion host, and no open inbound port 22 in the security group, which significantly shrinks the network attack surface. All session activity can be logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3 for security auditing, satisfying compliance requirements for recording privileged access. Any scenario emphasizing 'no open inbound ports' or 'no SSH keys to manage' for interactive troubleshooting access is describing Session Manager.

concepts.heading: Managed instance prerequisites
concepts.body: For an instance to be manageable by Systems Manager, it needs the SSM Agent installed and running (preinstalled on most current Amazon Linux and Windows AMIs) and an attached IAM role or instance profile granting the necessary SSM permissions, typically the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policy. On-premises or other-cloud servers can also be registered as managed instances using an activation code and the SSM Agent, extending the same tooling to hybrid environments. A common troubleshooting scenario on the exam is an instance that does not show up as 'Managed' in Systems Manager because it is missing the IAM role, not because of a network issue.

concepts.heading: Parameter Store for centralized configuration
concepts.body: Systems Manager Parameter Store centrally stores configuration data and secrets as hierarchical key-value parameters, which can be plain String, StringList, or SecureString (encrypted via KMS), and referenced by EC2 instances, Lambda functions, or CloudFormation templates instead of hardcoding values. This decouples configuration from application code and provides versioning and access control per parameter path, making it a lightweight alternative to Secrets Manager for values that do not need automatic rotation. On the exam, choose Parameter Store when the scenario is about simple, centrally managed configuration values, and Secrets Manager when automatic credential rotation is explicitly required.

examPoints: A scenario needing the same command run across hundreds of servers without SSH access is pointing to Systems Manager Run Command.

A scenario describing a multi-step operational procedure (create AMI, launch, verify, terminate old) that should run unattended is pointing to Systems Manager Automation, not a single Run Command execution.

quiz.q: An operations engineer needs to connect interactively to a production EC2 instance for troubleshooting, but company policy prohibits SSH keys and open inbound ports on production security groups. What should they use?
choices: A bastion host with a shared SSH key
A VPN with port 22 open only to the office IP
quiz.explain: Session Manager provides shell access over IAM permissions and the SSM Agent channel with no inbound ports required, satisfying the policy; a bastion host still requires SSH key management and an open port.

quiz.q: A team wants to automate a multi-step procedure that creates a new AMI from a running instance, launches a replacement, verifies it passes health checks, and then terminates the old instance, all without manual steps. Which Systems Manager capability fits this?
choices: Run Command with a single script
Systems Manager Automation using a runbook
quiz.explain: Automation runbooks orchestrate ordered, multi-step operational workflows across services; Run Command is designed for simpler, single-step command execution across a fleet.

days.recap: Run Command executes one-off commands across many servers; Automation orchestrates multi-step runbooks; Session Manager gives IAM-based shell access with no open ports; managed instances need the SSM Agent plus an IAM role; Parameter Store centralizes configuration.

days.title: Performance Optimization with Compute Optimizer and Trusted Advisor

concepts.heading: Compute Optimizer's data-driven recommendations
concepts.body: AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes the historical utilization metrics (CPU, memory when the CloudWatch agent is installed, network, and disk I/O) of EC2 instances, EBS volumes, Lambda functions, and Auto Scaling groups over a 14-day (or longer) lookback window, and uses machine learning to recommend better-fitting instance types or configurations. Recommendations are labeled with a risk level and estimated cost impact, distinguishing over-provisioned resources (wasting money) from under-provisioned ones (risking performance problems), which is more precise than manually eyeballing a CPU graph. This is the go-to service whenever a scenario asks for an automated, evidence-based way to right-size a fleet rather than a one-time manual review.

concepts.heading: Trusted Advisor's five-category checks
concepts.body: Trusted Advisor inspects an account against best practices across five categories — cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, and service limits — and returns simple green/yellow/red status checks with specific recommendations, such as identifying idle load balancers or S3 buckets with open access. The free Basic/Developer support tier only exposes a small subset of core checks (mainly security and service limits), while the full catalog of checks, along with programmatic access via the Trusted Advisor API, requires a Business or Enterprise support plan. Exam questions contrasting Trusted Advisor with Compute Optimizer usually hinge on breadth (many categories, shallower analysis) versus depth (deep, ML-driven sizing analysis for compute resources only).

concepts.heading: Right-sizing as an ongoing operational discipline
concepts.body: Right-sizing means continuously matching provisioned capacity to actual measured demand rather than sizing once at launch and never revisiting it, since workload patterns shift over time as traffic grows, features change, or usage becomes seasonal. Operationally this means periodically reviewing Compute Optimizer recommendations, applying safe changes (like resizing an instance during a maintenance window) and validating with CloudWatch metrics afterward, treating it as a recurring process rather than a single project. Right-sizing directly supports both of AWS's cost and performance pillars simultaneously, which is why it appears heavily in CloudOps-focused exam content.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing bottlenecks before optimizing
concepts.body: Before applying any sizing recommendation, an engineer should use CloudWatch metrics to identify which resource dimension is actually constrained — CPU, memory (via a custom or CloudWatch agent metric, since memory is not tracked by default for EC2), disk I/O, or network throughput — because resizing the wrong dimension wastes effort and money. For example, an application that is memory-bound will not improve by moving to a compute-optimized instance family; it needs a memory-optimized family or more RAM instead. This diagnostic step, done first, is what separates a correct right-sizing decision from a guess, and exam scenarios often embed a specific bottleneck clue that points to one instance family over another.

concepts.heading: Auto Scaling group recommendations
concepts.body: Compute Optimizer also evaluates entire Auto Scaling groups, not just individual instances, recommending a different instance type or a mixed-instance configuration when the group's scaling and utilization pattern suggests a better fit, which is particularly useful for workloads that scale horizontally. This differs from per-instance recommendations because it accounts for the group's overall demand curve rather than a single instance's history, and can suggest configurations that improve both elasticity and cost efficiency together. A scenario describing a fleet behind an Auto Scaling group that seems chronically over-provisioned is a strong hint toward reviewing Compute Optimizer's ASG-level recommendations.

examPoints: A scenario asking for a data-driven, ongoing recommendation on whether EC2 instances are over- or under-provisioned points to AWS Compute Optimizer.
A scenario asking for a broad best-practices check spanning cost, security, fault tolerance, performance, and service limits in one place points to AWS Trusted Advisor.

quiz.q: An operations team suspects several EC2 instances are significantly larger than needed based on actual usage, and wants an automated, metrics-based recommendation rather than manual guessing. Which service should they use?
quiz.explain: Compute Optimizer applies machine learning to historical utilization data specifically to recommend better-fitting instance sizes; Trusted Advisor's cost checks are more general and not as deeply tailored to instance-level right-sizing.

quiz.q: Which AWS tool provides best-practice checks across cost, performance, security, fault tolerance, and service limits in a single unified view?
quiz.explain: Trusted Advisor spans exactly these five categories with simple status indicators; Config focuses narrowly on configuration compliance rather than this broader best-practices scope.

days.recap: Compute Optimizer uses ML on historical metrics to recommend right-sized EC2/EBS/Lambda/ASG configurations; Trusted Advisor checks five best-practice categories account-wide; diagnose the actual bottleneck with CloudWatch before resizing.

days.title: Domain 1 Review: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, and Performance

concepts.heading: The detect-analyze-act framework
concepts.body: Domain 1's five days map cleanly onto a three-stage operational loop: detect (CloudWatch metrics and alarms, Config compliance checks), analyze (Logs Insights queries, CloudTrail event history), and act (EventBridge-triggered automation, Systems Manager runbooks). Thinking in this framework when reading a scenario question quickly narrows the candidate services, because the question's verb (monitor, investigate, or remediate) usually signals which stage it belongs to. Most real exam scenarios blend all three stages into a single narrative, so identifying which stage a specific sub-question is asking about is a key comprehension skill.

concepts.heading: Distinguishing overlapping detection services
concepts.body: CloudWatch alarms detect numeric threshold breaches, EventBridge rules detect discrete state-change events, Config Rules detect configuration drift from policy, and CloudTrail records the API calls behind any of those changes — four different signal types that are easy to confuse under exam time pressure. A fast way to disambiguate: if the question mentions a number and a threshold, think CloudWatch; if it mentions 'who performed the action,' think CloudTrail; if it mentions ongoing policy compliance of a resource's settings, think Config; if it mentions a specific AWS service event like a finding or state change, think EventBridge.

concepts.heading: Remediation service selection
concepts.body: Once a problem is detected, the corrective action is usually either an EC2-level action embedded in a CloudWatch alarm (stop/reboot/recover), a Systems Manager Automation runbook for anything more than a single step, or an SSM Run Command invocation for simple fleet-wide commands. Config Rules with attached remediation actions specifically close the loop for configuration drift, while GuardDuty findings routed through EventBridge close the loop for security threats. Recognizing which remediation tool matches which kind of detected problem is the second half of nearly every Domain 1 scenario question.

concepts.heading: Performance tools versus monitoring tools
concepts.body: Compute Optimizer and Trusted Advisor are forward-looking, advisory tools that recommend changes based on historical data, whereas CloudWatch and Config are always-on, real-time monitoring and compliance tools — mixing these categories up is a common source of wrong answers. A scenario asking 'is my fleet the right size' is a Compute Optimizer question, while a scenario asking 'alert me the instant CPU exceeds 90%' is a CloudWatch alarm question, even though both ultimately concern EC2 performance.

examPoints: When a scenario mixes multiple signals (a metric threshold plus a specific error log line plus a security finding), separate each clue and match it individually to CloudWatch, Logs, and EventBridge/GuardDuty respectively before choosing an answer.
Domain 1 is worth 22% of the exam, so budget review time proportionally and prioritize the CloudTrail vs. Config and Automation vs. Run Command distinctions, which recur most often.

quiz.q: Which service continuously evaluates whether resource configurations comply with a defined policy, such as requiring encryption on all EBS volumes?
quiz.explain: Config Rules continuously evaluate configuration compliance against policy; CloudTrail only logs the API calls that caused changes, without an ongoing pass/fail compliance judgment.

quiz.q: An operations team needs to run the same command across several hundred servers without establishing SSH connections to each one. What should they use?
choices: Session Manager, connecting to each server individually
quiz.explain: Run Command executes a command across many targeted instances in parallel through the SSM Agent channel; Session Manager is designed for interactive one-to-one shell sessions, not bulk command execution.

days.recap: Domain 1 wraps up: detect with CloudWatch/Config, analyze with Logs Insights/CloudTrail, act with EventBridge/Systems Manager, and separately use Compute Optimizer/Trusted Advisor for ongoing right-sizing advice.

days.title: Auto Scaling Mechanics and Scaling Policies

concepts.heading: Auto Scaling group capacity settings
concepts.body: An Auto Scaling group (ASG) is defined by minimum, maximum, and desired capacity, and it continuously enforces desired capacity by replacing any instance that fails its configured health check, which makes it the foundation of self-healing compute fleets. The group spans one or more Availability Zones and, by default, tries to balance instances evenly across them, so a single AZ failure only removes a portion of capacity rather than all of it. Setting minimum too low for a stateful or slow-starting application is a common exam trap, since it can leave the fleet unable to absorb a sudden load spike quickly enough.

concepts.heading: Scaling policy types
concepts.body: Target tracking scaling automatically adjusts capacity to keep a chosen metric, like average CPU utilization, at a target value, and is the simplest and most commonly recommended policy for variable, unpredictable load. Step scaling adjusts capacity by different amounts depending on how far a metric has breached a threshold (a larger breach adds more capacity at once), giving finer control for workloads with sharp, uneven spikes. Scheduled scaling proactively sets capacity ahead of a known time-based pattern, such as a daily 9 AM traffic surge, and is more efficient than reactive policies when the pattern is predictable, since capacity is already in place before demand arrives.

concepts.heading: Lifecycle hooks for graceful transitions
concepts.body: A lifecycle hook pauses an instance in a wait state during launch or termination, giving you time to run custom actions — such as pulling application dependencies before an instance enters service, or safely draining connections and uploading logs before an instance is terminated. Without a hook, an instance could be terminated mid-request or brought into service before it is actually ready to handle traffic, causing errors. Hooks typically integrate with EventBridge or SNS so a Lambda function can perform the custom work and then explicitly signal Auto Scaling to continue (CONTINUE) or abandon (ABANDON) the transition.

concepts.heading: Health check types
concepts.body: By default, an ASG uses the EC2 status check, which only detects underlying infrastructure failures, not application-level problems like a hung web server that still responds to ping but returns errors. Attaching an ELB health check instead (or in addition) lets the ASG detect application-layer failures reported by the load balancer's target health checks, and replace instances that are technically running but not functioning correctly. A scenario describing instances that 'look healthy at the infrastructure level but are failing application requests' is signaling the need for ELB health checks rather than the default EC2 check.

concepts.heading: Warm pools for faster scale-out
concepts.body: A warm pool keeps a set of pre-initialized instances in a stopped or running state outside of the active ASG capacity, ready to be moved into service much faster than launching and fully bootstrapping a brand-new instance from scratch. This is particularly useful for applications with long, expensive startup routines where target tracking's reactive scale-out would otherwise be too slow to meet demand. It trades a modest baseline cost (for the warm pool instances) for significantly reduced scale-out latency during sudden traffic increases.

examPoints: A scenario describing a known, recurring daily traffic spike where capacity should already be in place before it arrives is describing scheduled scaling, not target tracking.
A scenario needing time to safely upload logs or drain connections before an instance terminates is describing a lifecycle hook, not a termination policy.

quiz.q: A retail application reliably experiences a traffic surge every day at 9 AM when the market opens. Which Auto Scaling approach most efficiently prepares for this?
choices: Scheduled scaling that increases desired capacity shortly before 9 AM
Step scaling triggered after CPU exceeds 80%
Disabling Auto Scaling and using a fixed large fleet
quiz.explain: Scheduled scaling proactively provisions capacity ahead of a known pattern, avoiding the lag inherent in reactive policies like target tracking or step scaling, which only respond after the metric has already changed.

quiz.q: An Auto Scaling group needs to upload final application logs to S3 before an instance is terminated during scale-in. What should be configured?
choices: A lifecycle hook on the terminating transition
quiz.explain: A lifecycle hook pauses the termination process in a wait state, giving time to run the log upload before the instance is actually terminated; termination protection would instead prevent scale-in from removing the instance at all.

days.recap: ASGs enforce min/desired/max capacity with automatic replacement; target tracking, step, and scheduled scaling suit different load patterns; lifecycle hooks add custom pre-launch/pre-termination steps; ELB health checks catch app-layer failures the default EC2 check misses.

days.title: High Availability Design with Multi-AZ and Load Balancing

concepts.heading: Multi-AZ as the baseline for availability
concepts.body: Spreading an Auto Scaling group and its load balancer across at least two Availability Zones is the fundamental pattern for high availability, since each AZ is a physically separate facility with independent power, cooling, and networking, so a failure in one AZ should not take down the whole application. A single-AZ design, even with a large or redundant instance count, remains a single point of failure at the facility level, which is why exam scenarios describing 'the application must remain available if a data center has an outage' expect a multi-AZ answer rather than simply 'add more instances.'

concepts.heading: Load balancer health checks and traffic distribution
concepts.body: An Elastic Load Balancer continuously performs health checks against registered targets and automatically stops routing traffic to any target that fails, without needing manual intervention, which works hand-in-hand with Auto Scaling to keep only healthy instances serving requests. Application Load Balancers operate at layer 7 and can route based on path, host header, or other HTTP attributes, while Network Load Balancers operate at layer 4 for extreme performance and static IP requirements; picking the wrong type for a stated requirement (like needing a static IP, which points to NLB) is a classic exam distractor.

concepts.heading: Cross-zone load balancing
concepts.body: Cross-zone load balancing distributes incoming requests evenly across all registered targets in all enabled Availability Zones, rather than first distributing evenly across AZs and then evenly within each AZ, which matters when the number of instances differs significantly between zones. Without cross-zone balancing enabled, a zone with fewer instances could receive a disproportionately higher load per instance, creating uneven latency and potential overload in that zone even though overall capacity looks fine on paper. Application Load Balancers have this enabled by default, while Network Load Balancers require it to be explicitly turned on (and it may incur cross-AZ data transfer charges).

concepts.heading: EC2 placement groups
concepts.body: Placement groups influence how EC2 instances are physically positioned relative to each other: a cluster placement group packs instances close together on the same low-latency, high-throughput network segment for tightly coupled workloads like HPC, a spread placement group places a small number of instances on distinct underlying hardware to minimize simultaneous failure risk, and a partition placement group divides a larger set of instances into logical partitions with separate underlying hardware for large distributed systems like Hadoop or Cassandra. Choosing the wrong strategy for a stated goal — for example, using cluster placement when the requirement is actually fault isolation — is a common wrong-answer pattern.

concepts.heading: Validating availability with failover testing
concepts.body: A multi-AZ design is only as good as its last verified test, so operational best practice includes periodically simulating an AZ failure (for example, by temporarily removing one AZ's targets from the load balancer or deregistering an AZ's instances) to confirm the application continues serving traffic without manual intervention. Skipping this validation is a common root cause of surprise outages, because configuration drift or an overlooked hard dependency on a single-AZ resource (like a single-AZ RDS instance) can silently undermine an otherwise correct multi-AZ architecture.

examPoints: A scenario emphasizing that the application must survive a single data center (Availability Zone) outage is pointing toward deploying the ASG and load balancer across at least two AZs.
A scenario describing uneven load per instance across zones despite similar total target counts per zone is pointing toward enabling cross-zone load balancing.

quiz.q: A company's web application must continue serving traffic even if an entire Availability Zone becomes unavailable. What is the foundational design requirement to achieve this?
choices: Deploy a single, very large EC2 instance
Deploy the Auto Scaling group and load balancer across at least two Availability Zones
Use a single AZ with a bigger instance type
quiz.explain: Distributing compute and the load balancer across multiple AZs ensures that the failure of one physical facility does not remove all capacity; a bigger single instance in one AZ remains a single point of failure.

quiz.q: An operations engineer notices that one Availability Zone with fewer registered targets is experiencing much higher per-instance load than a zone with more targets, behind the same Network Load Balancer. What should they check?
choices: Whether cross-zone load balancing is enabled
Whether the security group allows inbound traffic
Whether the AMI is up to date
Whether the VPC has enough subnets
quiz.explain: Cross-zone load balancing distributes traffic evenly across all targets in all zones; NLBs have it disabled by default, which would exactly produce the described uneven per-instance load pattern.

days.recap: High availability starts with at least two AZs for compute and load balancer; ELB health checks remove unhealthy targets automatically; cross-zone load balancing evens per-instance load; placement groups control physical instance proximity; failover testing validates the design actually works.

days.title: Backup Strategy with AWS Backup and Snapshots

concepts.heading: AWS Backup for centralized policy management
concepts.body: AWS Backup provides a single place to define backup plans — schedules, retention rules, lifecycle transitions to cold storage, and cross-region or cross-account copy rules — that apply consistently across EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, S3, and other supported services, replacing a patchwork of per-service backup scripts and console clicks. Backup plans are attached to resources via tags or resource IDs, which makes it straightforward to enforce an organization-wide policy like 'every production-tagged resource gets daily backups retained for 35 days' without touching each service's individual console. This centralization is the answer whenever a scenario asks for a single, consistent backup policy spanning multiple AWS services.

concepts.heading: EBS snapshots and lifecycle automation
concepts.body: EBS snapshots are incremental, storing only the blocks that changed since the previous snapshot, and are saved to S3 behind the scenes, which keeps storage costs down for frequently snapshotted volumes even though each snapshot appears as a full point-in-time copy when restored. Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) automates the scheduled creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots based on tags, removing the need for custom scripts or Lambda functions to manage snapshot sprawl. Restoring from a snapshot creates a new volume, so exam scenarios about recovering a corrupted volume to a prior state usually expect 'create a new volume from a snapshot' rather than an in-place fix.

concepts.heading: RDS automated backups and point-in-time recovery
concepts.body: RDS automated backups take a daily full backup and continuously capture transaction logs, enabling point-in-time recovery (PITR) to any second within the configured retention window, up to a maximum of 35 days, which is essential for recovering from a logical error like an accidental DELETE rather than a full disaster. Restoring from an automated backup or PITR always creates a new RDS instance with a new endpoint, so a runbook needs a step to reconfigure application connection strings after restoration. Manual snapshots, by contrast, persist indefinitely until explicitly deleted and are useful for long-term retention outside the automated backup window.

concepts.heading: Backup Vault Lock for immutability
concepts.body: Backup Vault Lock applies a write-once-read-many (WORM) policy to a backup vault, preventing backups from being deleted or having their retention period shortened, even by an account's root user, once the lock is in compliance mode. This directly defends against ransomware scenarios where an attacker with administrative access tries to delete backups to prevent recovery, and against accidental deletion by an overly broad IAM policy. A governance mode lock can still be overridden by specific privileged users, while compliance mode cannot be reversed at all until the retention period expires, which is the distinction exam questions test.

concepts.heading: Choosing between backup approaches
concepts.body: The right backup mechanism depends on the recovery need: use AWS Backup for centralized, policy-driven backups spanning multiple services; use RDS PITR for recovering a database to a precise moment before a data corruption event; use EBS snapshots directly (often via DLM) for volume-level, infrastructure-focused recovery; and layer Backup Vault Lock on top of any of these when immutability against deletion is a stated requirement. Conflating 'backup frequency' requirements with 'point-in-time granularity' requirements is a common source of wrong answers, since PITR and daily snapshots solve different granularity problems.

examPoints: A scenario asking to manage backup policy for EBS, RDS, and DynamoDB from one place is asking for AWS Backup, not separate per-service scripts.
A scenario asking to restore a database to its exact state just before an accidental data deletion at a specific timestamp is asking for RDS point-in-time recovery.

quiz.q: An organization wants to centrally manage backup schedules and retention periods for its EBS volumes, RDS databases, and DynamoDB tables from a single policy rather than maintaining separate scripts per service. What should they use?
choices: AWS Backup with a unified backup plan
quiz.explain: AWS Backup lets a single backup plan apply consistent schedules and retention across multiple AWS services; managing separate scripts per service is exactly the operational overhead AWS Backup is designed to eliminate.

quiz.q: A database administrator needs to restore a production database to its exact state immediately before an accidental bulk delete that occurred at 3:07 PM yesterday. What is the appropriate recovery method?
choices: Restore the most recent manual snapshot only
Use RDS point-in-time recovery (PITR) to the moment just before 3:07 PM
Rebuild the database from application code
Restore only the latest EBS snapshot
quiz.explain: PITR uses continuous transaction logs to recover to a precise second, which is exactly what's needed to recover to just before the accidental delete; the most recent snapshot alone would likely already include the bad delete if taken afterward.

days.recap: AWS Backup centralizes policy across services; EBS snapshots are incremental and automated via DLM; RDS automated backups plus PITR give second-level recovery within the retention window; Backup Vault Lock adds WORM protection against deletion.

days.title: Disaster Recovery Strategy: RTO, RPO, and the Four DR Patterns

concepts.heading: Defining RTO and RPO
concepts.body: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable time between a disaster occurring and the application being restored to service, while Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured as a duration of time (for example, an RPO of 15 minutes means losing at most 15 minutes of data). These two numbers, defined by the business rather than the engineering team, drive every downstream architecture decision, so exam scenarios almost always give you specific RTO/RPO numbers and expect you to match them to the cheapest strategy that satisfies both.

concepts.heading: Backup and restore, and pilot light
concepts.body: Backup and restore is the lowest-cost, slowest-recovery strategy: data is backed up (often cross-region) but no standby infrastructure runs continuously, so recovery means provisioning infrastructure from scratch and restoring data, typically yielding an RTO measured in hours. Pilot light keeps only the most critical core components (often just a database, kept in sync via replication) running at minimal scale in the recovery region, with the rest of the application's infrastructure defined as code but not running, so recovery involves scaling up the pilot components and launching the remaining stack, improving RTO over backup and restore at a modest ongoing cost.

concepts.heading: Warm standby and multi-site active-active
concepts.body: Warm standby runs a scaled-down but fully functional copy of the entire application stack in the recovery region continuously, so failover just means scaling that environment up to full production capacity, giving a faster RTO than pilot light at a higher steady-state cost. Multi-site active-active runs full production capacity in two or more regions simultaneously, actively serving live traffic in normal operation (often via Route 53 or Global Accelerator routing), giving near-zero RTO and RPO at the highest cost, since you are effectively paying for two full production environments all the time.

concepts.heading: Matching strategy to requirements
concepts.body: As RTO and RPO requirements get stricter (shorter), the required DR strategy moves up the cost curve: backup and restore for RTO/RPO measured in hours, pilot light for tens of minutes to a couple of hours, warm standby for minutes, and multi-site active-active for near-zero. A well-designed exam answer picks the cheapest strategy that still satisfies the stated numbers — recommending multi-site active-active for a workload with a generous 24-hour RTO would be needlessly expensive and is a common wrong-answer trap in the other direction.

concepts.heading: Validating DR readiness with drills
concepts.body: A documented DR plan that has never been executed is not a reliable plan, so regularly scheduled DR drills — actually failing over to the secondary region or restoring from backups into a clean environment — are considered an operational best practice and are explicitly called out in AWS's Well-Architected guidance. Drills reveal gaps like missing IAM permissions in the DR region, out-of-date runbooks, or DNS records that were never actually configured to fail over, none of which show up just by reading the architecture diagram.

examPoints: A scenario stating an RTO of a few minutes with cost not being the primary constraint points to warm standby or multi-site active-active.
A scenario emphasizing cost sensitivity with an RTO/RPO of several hours points to backup and restore or pilot light, not the more expensive standby patterns.

quiz.q: A financial trading application requires an RTO of just a few minutes and cost is not the primary concern. Which DR strategy best fits this requirement?
quiz.explain: Multi-site active-active keeps full production capacity running in multiple regions simultaneously, providing the fastest possible failover; backup and restore or pilot light would both involve provisioning delays inconsistent with a few-minutes RTO.

quiz.q: A small internal reporting tool can tolerate several hours of downtime and does not have a large budget for redundant infrastructure. Which DR strategy is most cost-appropriate?
choices: Immediate failover with no data loss
quiz.explain: Backup and restore is the lowest-cost strategy and fits a several-hour RTO tolerance well; warm standby or active-active would introduce ongoing costs disproportionate to this workload's requirements.

days.recap: RTO caps downtime, RPO caps data loss; the four DR patterns (backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active-active) trade cost against recovery speed in that order; regular DR drills validate the plan actually works.

days.title: RDS and Aurora Resilience: Multi-AZ, Read Replicas, and Failover

concepts.heading: RDS Multi-AZ synchronous replication and failover
concepts.body: An RDS Multi-AZ deployment maintains a synchronously replicated standby instance in a different Availability Zone, and if the primary fails a health check, RDS automatically fails over to the standby, typically completing in one to two minutes, with the database's DNS endpoint automatically repointing to the new primary so applications do not need connection string changes. Because replication is synchronous, Multi-AZ provides high availability but essentially zero data loss on failover, making it the correct choice whenever a scenario asks specifically for automatic failover and durability against an AZ failure for RDS.

concepts.heading: Aurora's storage-level high availability
concepts.body: Aurora's storage layer is distributed across three Availability Zones with six-way replication by design (independent of whether you provision any Aurora Replicas), giving it very high durability and the ability to tolerate the loss of an entire AZ or up to two copies without losing data or write availability. When Aurora Replicas exist, failover to a replica is typically faster than an RDS Multi-AZ failover because Aurora Replicas share the same underlying storage volume as the primary and do not need to catch up via replication first. This storage architecture is a key differentiator that exam questions use to distinguish 'why Aurora over standard RDS' scenarios.

concepts.heading: Read replicas for performance versus DR
concepts.body: Read replicas use asynchronous replication and exist primarily to horizontally scale read traffic away from the primary instance, which is a performance optimization rather than a high-availability mechanism, since a read replica is not automatically promoted on primary failure. A read replica can be manually promoted to a standalone, writable instance, which makes it usable as part of a disaster recovery plan, but because replication is asynchronous, some in-flight transactions can be lost during promotion — a trade-off that must be weighed against the stricter zero-data-loss guarantee of Multi-AZ failover.

concepts.heading: Cross-region read replicas for regional DR
concepts.body: Cross-region read replicas replicate data asynchronously to another AWS region, allowing an application to promote the replica and resume operations there if the entire primary region becomes unavailable, addressing a failure scope that Multi-AZ (which only spans AZs within one region) cannot cover. This pattern is frequently the correct answer for scenarios explicitly describing a full regional outage requirement, whereas Multi-AZ alone is the correct answer for AZ-level outage requirements — conflating the two failure scopes is one of the most common Domain 2 exam mistakes.

concepts.heading: Choosing Multi-AZ, replicas, or both together
concepts.body: Production architectures commonly combine both: Multi-AZ for automatic, low-RPO failover against AZ failures, plus one or more read replicas (in the same region or cross-region) to offload read traffic and provide an additional DR option, since the two mechanisms solve different problems and are not mutually exclusive. On the exam, watch for scenarios that need both availability (keep serving traffic) and read scalability (handle more read load) simultaneously — this combination is the intended answer rather than picking only one feature.

examPoints: A scenario needing automatic failover with minimal data loss after an Availability Zone failure for RDS is asking for Multi-AZ, not read replicas.

A scenario needing the ability to continue operating after an entire region becomes unavailable is asking for a cross-region read replica (or cross-region backup strategy), not same-region Multi-AZ alone.

quiz.q: A production RDS database must automatically fail over with minimal data loss if its Availability Zone experiences an outage. What should be configured?
quiz.explain: Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication and automatic failover to a standby in a different AZ; a read replica alone uses asynchronous replication and does not fail over automatically.

quiz.q: A company wants to be able to resume database operations in a different AWS region if their primary region suffers a complete outage. What should they implement?
choices: A cross-region read replica that can be promoted
quiz.explain: A cross-region read replica can be promoted to a standalone writable database in another region, addressing a regional failure; Multi-AZ only protects against failures within a single region's Availability Zones.

days.recap: RDS Multi-AZ gives synchronous replication and automatic AZ-level failover; Aurora's 6-way multi-AZ storage gives strong durability with fast replica failover; read replicas are for read scaling (asynchronous) and can be promoted for DR; cross-region replicas address regional disasters.

days.title: Domain 2 Review: Reliability, Backup, and Disaster Recovery

concepts.heading: Availability versus recoverability
concepts.body: Domain 2 splits into two related but distinct concerns: availability mechanisms (Auto Scaling, Multi-AZ, load balancing) that keep an application running continuously through component failures, and recoverability mechanisms (backups, snapshots, DR strategies) that let you restore service and data after a more serious failure or data loss event. A scenario about 'staying up during a failure' calls for availability features, while a scenario about 'getting back a lost or corrupted state' calls for backup and recovery features, and questions often test whether you can tell which category a described symptom belongs to.

concepts.heading: Matching DR numbers to patterns quickly
concepts.body: Whenever a question states specific RTO/RPO numbers, immediately map them to the four-tier DR ladder (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active-active) rather than reasoning about DR strategy from scratch each time — this table lookup approach is faster and reduces errors under time pressure. Similarly, always identify first whether the failure scope described is an AZ failure or a full region failure, since that single distinction determines whether Multi-AZ is sufficient or a cross-region strategy is required.

concepts.heading: Scaling policy quick reference
concepts.body: For Auto Scaling, remember the three policy types map to three traffic shapes: target tracking for steady-state maintenance of a target metric, step scaling for uneven or bursty spikes needing proportionally larger responses, and scheduled scaling for known, time-based patterns — plus lifecycle hooks whenever a scenario needs custom work done during launch or termination transitions.

concepts.heading: Full domain 2 synthesis
concepts.body: Putting it together, a resilient CloudOps architecture layers Auto Scaling and Multi-AZ load balancing for continuous availability, RDS Multi-AZ or Aurora's storage architecture for database resilience, AWS Backup and snapshots for data protection, and a DR strategy sized to business RTO/RPO requirements for the worst-case regional scenario — each layer addressing a different failure mode rather than one mechanism doing everything.

examPoints: When a question gives specific RTO/RPO numbers, immediately match them against the four-tier DR strategy table rather than reasoning from first principles under time pressure.
Distinguish AZ-scope failures (solved by Multi-AZ) from region-scope failures (solved by cross-region replicas or a full DR strategy) as the very first step in any Domain 2 scenario.

quiz.q: Which Auto Scaling policy type proactively adjusts capacity ahead of a known, predictable traffic pattern?
quiz.explain: Scheduled scaling sets capacity changes in advance for known time-based patterns; target tracking and step scaling are both reactive, responding only after the metric has already changed.

quiz.q: An organization needs the shortest possible RTO and cost is not a limiting factor. Which DR strategy should they choose?
quiz.explain: Multi-site active-active provides the fastest possible recovery since full production capacity is already running in multiple regions; the other strategies all involve some provisioning or scale-up delay.

days.recap: Domain 2 wraps up: availability (ASG scaling policies, Multi-AZ, ELB) keeps the app running; backup and DR strategy (AWS Backup, snapshots, the four DR tiers, RDS Multi-AZ vs. replicas) restores it after a serious failure.

days.title: EC2 Image Management: AMIs and Launch Templates

concepts.heading: The golden AMI pattern
concepts.body: An Amazon Machine Image (AMI) packages an OS, installed software, and configuration into a reusable template that new EC2 instances launch from, and the golden AMI pattern means baking a fully configured, tested image once and reusing it everywhere, instead of running configuration scripts on every new instance at boot time. This significantly speeds up instance launch (since dependencies are already installed) and improves consistency across a fleet, though it introduces the operational responsibility of keeping the golden AMI itself patched and current, since instances launched from a stale AMI inherit stale software.

concepts.heading: AMI creation and cross-region/account copying
concepts.body: Creating an AMI from a running or stopped instance captures the root volume (and any attached EBS volumes) as a set of snapshots referenced by the AMI, and that AMI can then be copied to other regions or shared with other AWS accounts for multi-region deployment or organization-wide standardization. Copying an AMI to a new region creates independent snapshots there, so cross-region deployments do not depend on the original region being available, which matters for both deployment speed and disaster recovery scenarios.

concepts.heading: Launch templates versus launch configurations
concepts.body: A launch template specifies everything needed to launch an instance — AMI, instance type, security groups, key pair, user data, and more — and supports multiple versions, letting you update settings (like pointing to a newer AMI) while keeping older versions available for rollback or comparison. Launch templates are the current, actively developed mechanism and support features like multiple instance types and both On-Demand and Spot within a single Auto Scaling group, whereas the older launch configurations are immutable, single-version, and lack these newer capabilities, which is why AWS recommends launch templates for all new work.

concepts.heading: EC2 Image Builder for automated pipelines
concepts.body: EC2 Image Builder automates the entire AMI lifecycle — building an image from a base AMI plus a defined list of components (software installs, patches, configuration), automatically testing it, and distributing the resulting AMI to one or more regions — on a recurring schedule so that a fresh, patched AMI is produced automatically rather than requiring someone to manually rebuild and repatch an image periodically. This removes the operational toil and human error risk of manual AMI maintenance and is the correct answer whenever a scenario describes wanting patched images produced automatically on a schedule.

concepts.heading: Deprecating and cleaning up old AMIs
concepts.body: Because each AMI references underlying EBS snapshots that continue to incur storage charges, operational hygiene requires deregistering old, unused AMIs and deleting their associated snapshots, ideally automated via a lifecycle policy or Image Builder's built-in distribution and deprecation settings rather than left to accumulate indefinitely. Forgetting this cleanup step is a subtle but real cost-optimization issue that can surface in scenario questions about unexpectedly high EBS snapshot storage costs.

examPoints: A scenario needing hundreds of instances deployed with identical, pre-installed software and configuration quickly is describing the golden AMI pattern combined with a launch template.
A scenario wanting AMIs automatically rebuilt with the latest security patches on a recurring schedule, without manual intervention, is describing EC2 Image Builder.

quiz.q: A company needs to deploy hundreds of EC2 instances with an identical, pre-installed application stack as quickly as possible. What approach best supports this?
choices: Run a configuration script on every instance after boot
Create a golden AMI with the software pre-installed and launch instances from it via a launch template
Use only user data scripts with a base AMI
quiz.explain: A golden AMI already contains the fully configured software, so instances launch ready to serve immediately; relying solely on boot-time scripts adds startup latency and inconsistency risk across instances.

quiz.q: An operations team wants newly patched AMIs to be built, tested, and distributed automatically on a recurring schedule without manual rebuilding. Which service should they use?
choices: Manually create a new AMI every month
EC2 Image Builder with a defined pipeline and schedule
quiz.explain: EC2 Image Builder automates the build, test, and distribution of AMIs on a schedule; manually recreating AMIs does not scale and is error-prone.

days.recap: AMIs are reusable instance templates (golden AMI pattern); launch templates are the versioned, current way to define launch settings; EC2 Image Builder automates AMI build/test/distribution pipelines; clean up old AMIs and snapshots to control cost.

days.title: Container Operations: ECR and ECS Fundamentals

concepts.heading: ECR image storage and vulnerability scanning
concepts.body: Amazon ECR is a fully managed container registry for storing and versioning Docker and OCI images, with built-in image scanning (basic scanning using the open-source Clair-based engine, or enhanced scanning via Amazon Inspector integration) that automatically flags known CVEs in an image's layers, giving operations teams visibility into vulnerable base images or dependencies before they are deployed. Scan results can be forwarded through EventBridge for automated alerting, closing the loop between finding a vulnerability and notifying the responsible team.

concepts.heading: Lifecycle policies for image cleanup
concepts.body: ECR lifecycle policies automatically expire and remove old or untagged images based on rules such as 'keep only the last 10 tagged images' or 'expire untagged images after 14 days,' preventing a repository from accumulating unlimited historical image versions and the associated storage cost. Without lifecycle policies, every CI/CD build could push a new image indefinitely, and operations teams are expected to configure these policies proactively rather than manually pruning repositories.

concepts.heading: ECS task definitions and services
concepts.body: A task definition is a blueprint specifying which container image(s) to run, CPU/memory allocation, networking mode, and IAM permissions, while an ECS service maintains a specified number of running tasks from that definition, automatically replacing any task that stops unexpectedly, similar in spirit to how an ASG maintains EC2 instance count. This separation lets you version task definitions independently from the running service, and update the service to a new task definition revision to perform a deployment.

concepts.heading: Deployment strategies for zero downtime
concepts.body: ECS supports rolling updates, which replace old tasks with new ones incrementally, controlled by minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent settings that determine how much capacity can be temporarily reduced or over-provisioned during the rollout, and blue/green deployments via integration with CodeDeploy, which shift traffic to an entirely new task set only after it passes health checks, with the ability to quickly roll back by shifting traffic back. Blue/green is generally preferred when a scenario demands the ability to instantly roll back a bad deployment with zero impact to the old environment.

concepts.heading: Container Insights for observability
concepts.body: Container Insights collects and aggregates CPU, memory, network, and storage metrics at the cluster, service, and task level for both ECS and EKS, and surfaces them as CloudWatch dashboards and metrics, going well beyond the basic instance-level metrics that CloudWatch provides for the underlying EC2 hosts by themselves. This is the correct answer whenever a scenario specifically needs container- or task-level resource visibility rather than just host-level EC2 metrics.

examPoints: A scenario asking to automatically detect known vulnerabilities in container images before deployment is describing ECR image scanning.
A scenario asking for task- or container-level CPU/memory metrics rather than just EC2 host metrics is describing Container Insights.

quiz.q: A security team wants container images in ECR to be automatically checked for known vulnerabilities before they are deployed to production. What ECR feature addresses this?
quiz.explain: ECR's image scanning capability checks image layers for known CVEs; lifecycle policies only manage image retention and deletion, not vulnerability detection.

quiz.q: An operations team needs detailed CPU and memory metrics at the individual ECS task level, beyond what default EC2 host metrics provide. What should they enable?
quiz.explain: Container Insights aggregates task- and service-level resource metrics specifically for containerized workloads; default EC2 metrics only reflect the host, not individual containers or tasks.

days.recap: ECR stores and scans container images with lifecycle policies for cleanup; ECS task definitions define containers while services maintain desired task count; rolling and blue/green deployments both enable zero-downtime updates; Container Insights adds container-level observability.

days.title: Infrastructure as Code: CloudFormation and CDK Operations

concepts.heading: Drift detection for consistency verification
concepts.body: CloudFormation drift detection compares the current, actual state of a stack's resources against what the template defines, flagging any resource that was manually modified outside of CloudFormation (for example, someone changing a security group rule directly in the console) as having drifted. This matters operationally because manual out-of-band changes undermine the core IaC guarantee that the template is the single source of truth, and drift detection is the tool for discovering when that guarantee has silently been broken so it can be corrected or the template updated to match reality.

concepts.heading: StackSets for multi-account, multi-region deployment
concepts.body: CloudFormation StackSets extend a single template to deploy and manage consistent stacks across many AWS accounts and regions from one operation, which is the standard mechanism for rolling out organization-wide baselines like mandatory logging configuration, security guardrails, or standard IAM roles to every account in an AWS Organization. StackSets can integrate directly with AWS Organizations for automatic deployment to new accounts as they are created, removing the need to manually apply the baseline to every new account.

concepts.heading: CDK Pipelines and self-mutation
concepts.body: The AWS CDK lets you define infrastructure using a general-purpose programming language (TypeScript, Python, Java, etc.), which CDK synthesizes into CloudFormation templates under the hood, giving you loops, conditionals, and reusable constructs that plain CloudFormation templates lack. CDK Pipelines defines the CI/CD pipeline that deploys your infrastructure using CDK code itself, and is 'self-mutating' — meaning that if a pipeline update changes the pipeline's own structure, the pipeline automatically updates itself as part of its own execution, without requiring a separate manual pipeline redeployment step.

concepts.heading: IaC provisioning versus SSM operational automation
concepts.body: CloudFormation and CDK answer 'how should this resource be created and configured' (the desired end-state definition of infrastructure), while Systems Manager Automation answers 'what operational task should be performed on a resource that already exists' (like patching or restarting) — a scenario about creating new infrastructure consistently points to IaC, while a scenario about operating on already-existing infrastructure points to SSM, and confusing the two categories is a common source of wrong answers on Domain 3 questions.

concepts.heading: Change sets for safe stack updates
concepts.body: Before actually applying an update to a running CloudFormation stack, a change set previews exactly which resources will be modified, replaced, or deleted, letting an operator verify that an update will not unexpectedly replace (and therefore delete and recreate) a critical resource like a database before committing to the change. This preview-before-apply workflow is a key safety practice for production stack updates and is the mechanism the exam expects you to know for avoiding unintended resource replacement.

examPoints: A scenario asking to detect whether someone manually changed a resource outside of CloudFormation, differing from the template, is describing drift detection.
A scenario asking to deploy and continuously manage an identical baseline template across dozens of AWS accounts and regions is describing CloudFormation StackSets.

quiz.q: An organization needs to deploy an identical security baseline template to fifty AWS accounts across three regions and keep them all in sync going forward. What should they use?
choices: Manually deploy the template to each account
A single CloudFormation stack in one account
quiz.explain: StackSets are purpose-built for deploying and managing the same template consistently across many accounts and regions from a single operation; manual per-account deployment does not scale and is error-prone.

quiz.q: An engineer suspects someone manually changed a resource's configuration directly in the console, causing it to differ from what the CloudFormation template defines. How can this be confirmed?
choices: Run CloudFormation drift detection on the stack
quiz.explain: Drift detection specifically compares actual resource state to the template's defined state and reports discrepancies; deleting and recreating the stack is destructive and unnecessary just to detect the issue.

days.recap: Drift detection finds manual changes that diverge from the template; StackSets deploy one template across many accounts/regions; CDK Pipelines self-mutate; IaC (CloudFormation/CDK) provisions resources while SSM automates operations on existing ones; change sets preview updates safely.

days.title: Systems Manager Automation: State Manager and Patch Manager

concepts.heading: State Manager for continuous configuration enforcement
concepts.body: State Manager continuously applies and re-applies a defined configuration state (such as ensuring a specific agent is installed, a configuration file has certain content, or a Windows feature is enabled) to managed instances on a schedule, automatically correcting any drift that occurs between enforcement runs. This differs from a one-time Run Command execution because State Manager keeps checking and re-applying indefinitely, making it the right answer whenever a scenario emphasizes instances needing to 'always' or 'continuously' maintain a particular state rather than a single corrective action.

concepts.heading: Patch Manager, baselines, and maintenance windows
concepts.body: Patch Manager automates scanning instances for missing patches and installing approved ones according to a patch baseline, which defines rules for which patches are auto-approved (for example, security patches classified Critical, auto-approved after 7 days) versus which require explicit approval, giving operations teams policy-driven control over the patching cadence rather than all-or-nothing automatic updates. Patching actions are typically scheduled inside a maintenance window, a defined recurring time range chosen to minimize business impact, during which Patch Manager (or other registered tasks) is allowed to run against the target instances.

concepts.heading: Maintenance windows for controlled operational timing
concepts.body: A maintenance window specifies both the schedule (when) and the targets and tasks (what, and on which instances) for potentially disruptive operations like patching or restarts, ensuring these actions only happen during an approved low-impact period rather than during peak business hours. Multiple tasks (patching, running a specific SSM document, invoking a Lambda function) can be registered against the same maintenance window, centralizing when disruptive operational work is allowed to occur across a fleet.

concepts.heading: Systems Manager Inventory for asset visibility
concepts.body: Inventory collects metadata from managed instances — installed applications, OS version, network configuration, and more — into a centrally queryable dataset, which supports both operational needs (knowing exactly what software versions are deployed where) and compliance needs (proving which instances have or have not received a required software update). This is distinct from Config, which tracks AWS resource configuration; Inventory specifically focuses on what is installed and configured inside the operating system of a managed instance.

concepts.heading: Compliance reporting across the patch fleet
concepts.body: Patch Manager and State Manager both report per-instance compliance status back to Systems Manager Compliance, giving a single dashboard view of which instances are fully patched or in the desired state versus which are lagging, which supports both day-to-day operations and audit reporting. A scenario asking for a dashboard-style view of 'how many servers are missing critical patches right now' is pointing to this compliance reporting rather than manually checking each instance.

examPoints: A scenario needing OS security patches applied on a recurring basis, with visibility into overall compliance, is describing Patch Manager plus maintenance windows.
A scenario needing a server's configuration to be continuously enforced and self-corrected over time, not just fixed once, is describing State Manager.

quiz.q: An organization needs OS security patches automatically scanned for and applied across hundreds of instances on a recurring, policy-driven schedule, with compliance visible on a dashboard. What should they configure?
choices: Systems Manager Patch Manager with a patch baseline and maintenance window
quiz.explain: Patch Manager automates scanning and patch application according to a defined baseline within a scheduled maintenance window, and reports compliance centrally; manual patching does not scale to hundreds of instances reliably.
